a: Put the table on the north side.
t: Where do the incense altar instructions go?
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch and a Dead Sea scroll move 30:1–10 (the incense altar) to follow this verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint; all English versions
readings.en: and the table you shall put on the north side
readings.plain: Put the table on the north side.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch; 4QpaleoExod-m, a Dead Sea scroll in the old Hebrew script (first century BC)
readings.en: the instructions for the incense altar follow
readings.plain: Put the table on the north side. [These witnesses place here the instructions for the incense altar, 30:1–10, instead of in chapter 30.]

why: Most scholars, including Emanuel Tov and Judith Sanderson, think the Samaritan and Qumran order is a later editorial improvement: someone noticed that the incense altar was missing where the other furnishings are described and moved it there. The Masoretic order is the harder reading and is shared by the Greek. The different placement shows that scribes before Jesus felt free to rearrange this section.
b: 4QpaleoExod-m is one of the longest Exodus scrolls from Qumran. It often agrees with the Samaritan Pentateuch against the Masoretic Text in longer, harmonizing readings, though it lacks the specifically Samaritan changes about Mount Gerizim.

t: A command for the priests' woven clothes
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch and the Qumran scroll 4QpaleoExod-m add a command here to make the woven clothes for service, which 39:1 says were made.

readings.en: bronze
readings.plain: are to be bronze.

readings.orig: נחשת ועשית בגדי תכלת וארגמן ותולעת שני לשרת בהם בקדש
readings.en: bronze. And you shall make garments of blue, purple and scarlet to serve in them in the holy place
readings.plain: are to be bronze. Make clothes of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, for serving in the holy place.

why: In 39:1 the craftsmen make "woven clothes for serving in the holy place," but no verse in chapters 25–31 commands them in those words. The Samaritan Pentateuch and 4QpaleoExod-m supply the missing command, a typical case of their habit of making command and fulfillment match exactly. The Masoretic Text, which leaves the gap, is more likely original.

p: 4QpaleoExod-m and the Samaritan Pentateuch lack the words 'spread with oil' here.

readings.en: anointed with oil
readings.plain: spread with oil

readings.en: (the words are absent)

why: The wafers spread with oil appear again in the rite itself (29:23) and in Leviticus 2:4 and 8:26, so the words are at home here. Their absence in the scroll and the Samaritan text is more likely a scribe's slip than the original reading. The difference does not change the rite.

a: Take some of the blood that is on the altar and some of the anointing oil
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch and 4QpaleoExod-m place this verse after 29:28, so the sprinkling follows the waving.

readings.orig: וְלָקַחְתָּ מִן־הַדָּם אֲשֶׁר עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וּמִשֶּׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה
readings.en: and you shall take some of the blood that is on the altar and some of the anointing oil
readings.plain: Take some of the blood that is on the altar and some of the anointing oil

readings.en: the verse comes after the waving and the priests' share
readings.plain: Take some of the blood that is on the altar and some of the anointing oil [These witnesses place this verse after 29:28.]

why: In Leviticus 8, where Moses carries out this rite, the sprinkling of blood and oil on the priests comes after the waving and the burning (Leviticus 8:30). The Samaritan and Qumran order matches that account, which is the kind of harmonizing these witnesses often do. The Masoretic order, which interrupts the ram ritual, is the harder reading and probably the older one.

a: Then I will make you into a great nation.
p: The Samaritan text and a Qumran scroll add here that God was angry with Aaron and Moses prayed for him (Deuteronomy 9:20).

readings.en: and I will make you a great nation
readings.plain: Then I will make you into a great nation.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch; 4QpaleoExod-m (partly preserved, the rest restored from the Samaritan)
readings.orig: ... וּבְאַהֲרֹן הִתְאַנַּף יְהוָה מְאֹד לְהַשְׁמִידוֹ וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל מֹשֶׁה בְּעַד אַהֲרֹן
readings.en: ... And the LORD was very angry with Aaron, to destroy him, and Moses prayed for Aaron
readings.plain: Then I will make you into a great nation." The LORD was very angry with Aaron, enough to destroy him, and Moses prayed for Aaron.

why: The added sentence is taken almost word for word from Deuteronomy 9:20, where Moses remembers this event. Scribes of the Samaritan tradition often copied details from Deuteronomy back into Exodus so that the two accounts matched. The shorter Masoretic and Greek text is very likely original. The addition shows that ancient readers already noticed that Exodus says nothing about Aaron's punishment.

a: It is the sound of singing that I hear.
p: The Greek reads 'the sound of those who start up over wine' instead of 'singing.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum Onkelos; KJV and most English versions
readings.en: the sound of singing I hear
readings.plain: It is the sound of singing that I hear.

readings.en: the sound of those leading off with wine I hear
readings.plain: It is the noise of men starting up over their wine that I hear.

why: The Hebrew word is rare and its form unusual, and the Greek translators seem to have guessed from the context of a feast (32:6) or read a slightly different Hebrew word. The Masoretic reading fits the wordplay of the whole verse, built on the verb 'anah (see the note).

p: The consonants say 'his hand'; the Masoretes' reading tradition says 'his hands.'

readings.w: Qere (the reading tradition of the Masoretes); most versions
readings.en: from his hands
readings.plain: from his hands

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants of the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: from his hand
readings.plain: from his hand

why: The difference is one letter and changes nothing in the meaning (in 32:15 the Hebrew has "in his hand"). Several other Ketiv/Qere pairs in these chapters (27:11; 28:28; 32:17; 35:11; 37:8; 39:4; 39:33) are similar singular/plural or spelling differences and need no separate entry.

a: Fill your hands today for the LORD
p: The Hebrew says 'fill your hands' (a command). The Greek and Latin say 'you have filled your hands.'

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), imperative mil'u; KJV ("Consecrate yourselves today")
readings.en: fill your hands today for the LORD
readings.plain: Fill your hands today for the LORD

readings.w: Septuagint (eplērōsate), Latin Vulgate (consecrastis); many modern versions
readings.orig: ἐπληρώσατε τὰς χεῖρας ὑμῶν σήμερον κυρίῳ
readings.en: you have filled your hands today for the Lord
readings.plain: Today you have filled your hands for the LORD

why: The Masoretic Text vowels the word as an imperative, mil'u, "fill your hands." The Greek and Latin have "you have filled," which reflects either a different Hebrew form (mille'tem) or a free rendering of the same text. Some scholars read the consonants as a perfect. Most modern versions follow the sense of the ancient versions, because the Levites' action has already happened and Moses seems to be praising it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Masoretic vowels, which make Moses call the Levites to take up their new office. Either way, the Levites' loyalty marks them for God's service (Deuteronomy 33:8–11).

p: The Hebrew form here is odd. The Greek, Latin and Targums read 'the males,' and most scholars correct the Hebrew to match.

readings.w: Septuagint (ta arsenika); Theodotion; Latin Vulgate; Targums; most modern versions (correcting the Hebrew to hazzakhar)
readings.en: the males
readings.plain: every male among your livestock

readings.en: and all your livestock, it will be remembered (or: that bears a male)
readings.plain: and of all your livestock that bears a male

why: As written, the Masoretic tizzakhar looks like a form of the verb 'remember,' which makes no sense here. Traditional Jewish readers explained it as 'that bears a male' (so the KJV, 'that is male'). Most scholars think a scribe miscopied hazzakhar, 'the male,' since the ancient versions read that and the law about firstborn males in 13:12 says the same thing. Either way the meaning is that firstborn males belong to the LORD.

a: All the skilled at heart among those doing the work made the tabernacle
p: The Septuagint tells the building in a different order and much more briefly. Scholars still debate why.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch; the Qumran fragments of these chapters (4QpaleoExod-m, 4QExod-Lev-f, 2QExod-a and 2QExod-b) where preserved
readings.en: and every skilled person made
readings.plain: All the skilled at heart among those doing the work made the tabernacle

readings.w: Septuagint (Old Greek), chapters 36–39 in Greek numbering
readings.en: the priests' clothes are described first; the tent follows in short form
readings.plain: [In the Greek, the making of the priests' clothes (Hebrew 39:1–31) comes first. Then comes a short account of the curtains, veil and screen, without the goat-hair tent, the coverings, the frames or the bars (Hebrew 36:10–34).] All the skilled at heart among those doing the work made the tabernacle

why: This is the largest text-critical question in Exodus. In chapters 25–31 the Greek follows the Hebrew closely. In 35–40 it puts the priestly clothes first, then the tent and court, then the ark, table and lampstand, then the altar and basin, then the metal totals; it omits the incense altar from the building account (Hebrew 37:25–28) and many repeated details. Three main explanations are offered. D. W. Gooding (1959) argued that a later Greek editor rearranged a translation made from a text like the Masoretic one. John Wevers argued that the translator himself worked from a Hebrew text much like the Masoretic one and deliberately shortened and reordered it. Anneli Aejmelaeus, with Pierre-Maurice Bogaert, and in different ways Emanuel Tov and Eugene Ulrich, think the Greek was made from a different Hebrew text, perhaps an earlier "variant literary edition" of these chapters. Martha Wade found that the same translator produced both tabernacle accounts with a consistent technique, which tells against a later reworking in Greek. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text, which the Samaritan and Qumran evidence supports.
b: The Greek of the breastpiece instructions (Hebrew 28:23–29) is also shorter and arranged differently. The exact match between the Greek and Hebrew chapters is complicated, and Wevers' Notes on the Greek Text of Exodus sets it out in full.

a: He made the altar of incense of acacia wood.
t: No incense altar in the Greek building account
p: The Septuagint does not tell of making the incense altar (37:25–28). This entry and the next three verses go together.

readings.en: and he made the altar of incense
readings.plain: He made the altar of incense of acacia wood.

readings.en: (omitted)

why: The Greek building account mentions the anointing oil and incense (Hebrew 37:29) but not the gold altar, though the altar appears in the Greek of chapter 30 and of 40:5 and 40:26. Some think the omission is part of the Greek editor's shortening; others think the Hebrew text behind the Greek lacked it, which would fit the theory that the incense altar entered these chapters late (see the note on 26:35). The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text. The same omission covers 37:26–28.

t: Women who served, fasted or prayed?
p: The Hebrew says the women 'served' at the tent. The Greek says they 'fasted'; the Targum says they came to pray.

readings.en: the women who served
readings.plain: women who served

readings.en: the women who fasted
readings.plain: women who fasted

readings.en: the women who came to pray
readings.plain: women who came to pray

why: The Hebrew verb tsava' is used of organized service, including the Levites' work at the tent (Numbers 4:23), and 1 Samuel 2:22 uses the same phrase. The Greek and Aramaic translators seem to have understood the women's service as devotion, fasting or prayer, perhaps because women did not serve as priests. Their readings are interpretations of the same Hebrew rather than evidence of a different text. Luke's picture of Anna, who "never left the temple, serving God with fasting and prayer" (Luke 2:37), shows that this understanding was current in Jesus' day.

a: just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch adds that they made the Urim and Thummim, which the Hebrew never says.

readings.en: as the LORD commanded Moses
readings.plain: just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

readings.orig: כאשר צוה יהוה את משה ויעשו את האורים ואת התמים כאשר צוה יהוה את משה
readings.en: as the LORD commanded Moses. And they made the Urim and the Thummim, as the LORD commanded Moses
readings.plain: just as the LORD had commanded Moses. They made the Urim and the Thummim, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

why: The Urim and Thummim are to be put into the breastpiece (28:30), but the building account never says they were made, and Leviticus 8:8 simply has Moses put them in. The Samaritan text fills the gap, as it often does. The Masoretic silence is more likely original and may mean that the Urim and Thummim were not crafted objects at all but something already in existence.

a: in the first month of the second year
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and 4QExod-Lev-f add 'of their coming out of Egypt.'

readings.en: in the first month in the second year
readings.plain: in the first month of the second year

readings.orig: τῷ δευτέρῳ ἔτει ἐκπορευομένων αὐτῶν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου
readings.en: in the second year of their coming out of Egypt
readings.plain: in the first month of the second year after they came out of Egypt

why: The longer reading spells out what the date means, in words like those of Numbers 1:1 and 9:1. Additions that make a date clearer are typical of the Samaritan tradition and its relatives, and the shorter Masoretic text is probably original. The meaning is the same: the tabernacle was raised almost exactly a year after the exodus.
